_about: Short explanations written for this project, used in the Meaning section where no commentary exists for a verse or its neighbours.

en.1.6: Duryodhana continues listing the Pandava champions, now naming the younger generation: Abhimanyu, son of Arjuna and Subhadra, and the five sons of Draupadi. His long roll call shows how anxious he is. Instead of trusting his own vast army, he keeps measuring himself against the strength of the other side.
en.1.7: Having listed the enemy's heroes, Duryodhana turns to his own side to reassure his teacher Drona and, really, himself. Leaders who feel insecure often talk up their resources out loud. The scene shows a mind that depends on outside strength rather than inner conviction.
en.1.8: Duryodhana names his great commanders: Drona himself, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashwatthama, Vikarna and Bhurishravas. These were among the most respected warriors of the age. Many of them fought for him out of duty or obligation rather than belief in his cause, which is part of the tragedy of the war.
en.1.12: Seeing Duryodhana's nervousness, the elder Bhishma roars like a lion and blows his conch to lift his spirits. It is an act of loyalty and encouragement from the grand old man of the family. The conch blast also formally signals that the battle is about to begin.
en.1.13: The whole Kaurava army answers Bhishma at once with conches, drums and horns, creating a deafening roar. The noise is meant to raise courage and frighten the enemy. Sanjaya describes the sound as tremendous, setting the charged atmosphere of the battlefield.
en.1.14: Now Krishna and Arjuna, standing in their magnificent chariot drawn by white horses, blow their divine conches. The white horses suggest purity and the divine conches suggest that this side has grace on its side. With Krishna as Arjuna's charioteer, the stage is set for the dialogue that follows.
en.1.15: Each hero's conch has its own name, like a personal emblem. Krishna blows Panchajanya, Arjuna blows Devadatta, and the mighty Bhima blows Paundra. Naming them honours each warrior and shows the Pandavas answering the Kauravas with confidence.
en.1.16: The other Pandava brothers join in. Yudhishthira, the eldest, blows Anantavijaya, meaning endless victory, while the twins Nakula and Sahadeva blow Sughosha and Manipushpaka. The whole family stands united, each brother adding his voice.
en.1.20: Arjuna, whose flag carries the image of Hanuman, sees the Kaurava army lined up and raises his bow as the first weapons are about to fly. Hanuman on the flag is a symbol of strength, devotion and divine protection. This is the last moment of certainty before Arjuna's crisis begins.
en.1.21: Arjuna asks Krishna to drive his chariot to the space between the two armies. Krishna, the Lord himself, has humbly taken the role of charioteer and follows his friend's instruction. Arjuna wants to see the battlefield clearly, not knowing that the view will shake him to the core.
en.1.22: Arjuna explains why he wants to stand between the armies: he wants to see exactly who he must fight. On the surface it is a warrior's practical wish to size up the enemy. Underneath, it sets up the moment when he recognises the faces of his own family.
en.1.23: Arjuna wants to see those who have gathered to support Duryodhana, whom he calls evil-minded. He still sees the battle in clear terms of right and wrong. That clarity is about to dissolve when he looks at the people standing there.
en.1.24: Krishna does as Arjuna asks and places the chariot in the middle of the battlefield. Sanjaya narrates this to the blind King Dhritarashtra, who is hearing the whole story second-hand. Krishna chooses the spot carefully, right in front of the elders Arjuna loves most.
en.1.25: Positioned before Bhishma and Drona, Krishna simply says, "Arjuna, look at the Kurus gathered here." The words are few, but deliberate. By asking Arjuna to look, Krishna brings his hidden attachments to the surface so they can be addressed.
en.1.26: Arjuna looks and sees fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends on both sides. The enemy is no longer a faceless army. It is his own family and the people who raised and taught him.
en.1.27: Seeing fathers-in-law and dear friends in both armies, Arjuna is overwhelmed. This is the turning point of the chapter. The warrior's resolve gives way to personal grief as he sees relationships rather than opponents.
en.1.28: Arjuna is filled with compassion and despair and begins to speak. The Gita describes his state as pity mixed with confusion. His feeling is human and understandable, but as Krishna will show, it is clouding his judgement about his duty.
en.1.29: Arjuna describes his body giving way: his limbs feel weak, his mouth is dry, he is trembling and his hair stands on end. These are vivid signs of acute anxiety. The Gita does not hide the hero's breakdown; it starts the teaching exactly there.
en.1.30: His great bow Gandiva slips from his hand, his skin burns, he cannot stand steady and his mind spins. The strongest warrior of his time is completely overwhelmed. The verse shows that physical strength is no protection when the mind is in turmoil.
en.1.31: Arjuna says he sees only bad omens and can find no good in killing his own people. His mind now looks for reasons to support what his emotions already feel. This is a common pattern: when we are distressed, we read the signs to confirm our fears.
en.1.32: Arjuna says he wants no victory, kingdom or pleasure, and asks what any of it is worth. It sounds like renunciation, but it comes from grief rather than wisdom. Krishna will later teach the difference between letting go out of clarity and giving up out of despair.
en.1.33: Arjuna points out that the very people for whom one wants a kingdom and its joys are standing here, ready to give up their lives and wealth. Without them, success would feel empty. His love for his family is real, which is what makes his dilemma so painful.
en.1.34: Arjuna lists teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, uncles, in-laws and other relatives, all standing ready to fight. He sees every one of them as his own. The repetition of family words shows how personal the war has become for him.
en.1.42: Arjuna argues that the collapse of family order harms everyone, even the ancestors, who would lose the rites and offerings meant for them. He is using tradition and religion to justify his reluctance to fight. His reasoning is sincere, but it is driven by grief.
en.1.43: Arjuna continues that those who destroy families also destroy long-standing traditions and social values. He fears the war will leave society without its moral anchors. The concern is serious, but Krishna will show that abandoning his duty is not the answer.
en.1.44: Arjuna cites what he has heard: those who destroy family traditions suffer for a long time afterwards. He is building a case from scripture and custom. Fear of consequences now dominates his thinking.
en.1.45: Arjuna cries out that they are about to commit a great wrong just to win a kingdom and its pleasures. Guilt has taken over completely. He frames the whole war as selfish ambition, forgetting the injustice that made it necessary.
en.1.46: Arjuna says it would be better if the Kauravas killed him while he stood unarmed and did not resist. This is the lowest point of his despair. He would rather give up his life than face the choice in front of him.
en.1.47: Having spoken, Arjuna drops his bow and arrows and sinks down in the chariot, overwhelmed with sorrow. The first chapter ends with the hero collapsed. This is called the yoga of Arjuna's despair because the crisis itself becomes the doorway to wisdom.
en.2.1: Sanjaya describes Arjuna overcome with pity, his eyes full of tears, deeply distressed. It is to this broken Arjuna that Krishna now speaks. The teaching of the Gita begins not in a calm classroom but in a moment of real crisis.
en.2.2: Krishna's first words are a challenge: where has this weakness come from at such a critical moment? He says it does not suit a noble person and leads neither to honour nor to the higher good. Before offering comfort, Krishna shakes Arjuna out of his spiral.
en.2.3: Krishna urges Arjuna not to give in to faint-heartedness, saying it does not befit him. He tells him to shake off this weakness of heart and stand up. It is a call to remember who he really is and to act from strength rather than fear.
en.2.4: Arjuna replies by asking how he could possibly shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, who deserve his worship. His question is honest. He cannot reconcile his duty as a warrior with his love and reverence for his elders.
en.2.5: Arjuna says it would be better to live by begging than to kill his revered teachers. Any wealth or pleasure won by their death would feel stained with blood. His values are sincere, but they are being tested by a situation with no easy answer.
en.2.6: Arjuna admits he does not even know which outcome would be better, winning or losing. If he kills his cousins, he would not want to live. This uncertainty is the heart of his crisis and the reason he finally turns to Krishna for help.
en.2.7: Arjuna confesses that weakness and confusion have overpowered him and asks Krishna to tell him clearly what is best. He says, "I am your disciple; teach me, I surrender to you." This moment of humility transforms the conversation. Krishna's teaching begins because Arjuna asks.
en.2.8: Arjuna says that even a flourishing kingdom on earth or rule over the gods would not remove the grief drying up his senses. He has realised that outer success cannot heal inner pain. That realisation opens him to deeper wisdom.
en.2.9: Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, after speaking, declares "I will not fight" and falls silent. He has said everything he can. His silence makes space for Krishna's teaching to begin.
en.11.30: Arjuna sees the cosmic form consuming entire worlds with flaming mouths, its fiery radiance filling the universe. He is witnessing time and destruction as part of the divine. The image is terrifying, but it shows that every ending also lies within the Lord's power.
en.1.2: Sanjaya begins his report. Seeing the Pandava army arranged for battle, Duryodhana goes straight to his teacher Drona. Though he is king, he seeks out his teacher first, which hints at his unease. The story of the Gita opens with a leader who is worried before the fight has even started.
en.1.3: Duryodhana points out the Pandava army, organised by Dhrishtadyumna, son of Drupada and once Drona's own student. There is a sting in his words: Drona trained the very man now leading the enemy. Duryodhana is subtly questioning his teacher's loyalty to rouse him.
en.1.5: Duryodhana keeps naming great warriors on the Pandava side: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the king of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Shaibya. Each name adds to his sense of threat. The list shows how the Pandavas, though fewer, have gathered many respected allies.
en.1.9: Duryodhana adds that many other heroes are ready to give their lives for him, all skilled with many weapons. He takes comfort in the loyalty of others. Yet a confidence that rests entirely on other people's sacrifice is fragile.
en.1.11: Duryodhana orders all his commanders to hold their positions and protect Bhishma above everything. His whole strategy rests on one elder. It reveals both his respect for Bhishma's power and his fear of what happens without him.
en.1.17: Sanjaya continues naming the Pandava allies who blow their conches: the king of Kashi, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata and the unconquerable Satyaki. The roll call shows a united army answering with one voice.
en.1.19: The roar of the Pandava conches echoes across earth and sky and shakes the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons. A smaller army, united and confident, unsettles a larger one. Sanjaya hints to the blind king that his sons' courage is already wavering.
en.1.35: Arjuna says he would not kill his kinsmen even if they tried to kill him, not even for rule over the three worlds, let alone this earth. His love overrides any thought of gain. It is a noble feeling, but it leaves no room for his responsibility to stand against injustice.
en.1.37: Arjuna concludes that it is not right to kill their own relatives, asking how they could ever be happy after that. He measures the choice only by how it will feel afterwards. Krishna will later teach him to judge action by duty rather than by expected happiness.
en.1.38: Arjuna acknowledges that the Kauravas, blinded by greed, see nothing wrong in destroying their family or betraying friends. He believes that seeing the wrong clearly should keep him from joining in. His logic sounds moral, but it ignores that standing aside also has consequences.
en.1.41: Arjuna warns that when lawlessness spreads, the moral fabric of families weakens and social order breaks down. He is worried about the long-term damage war does to society. The fear is genuine, though it is being used to justify walking away from his duty.
en.2.10: Sanjaya tells the king that Krishna, standing between the two armies, smiles gently and speaks to the grieving Arjuna. The smile is not mockery but calm reassurance. Krishna can see beyond the crisis to the clarity Arjuna is about to gain.
en.2.17: Krishna points to the reality that pervades everything and says it can never be destroyed. Bodies and situations change, but that underlying presence does not. No one has the power to destroy the imperishable. This is the first step in removing Arjuna's grief about death.
en.2.22: Krishna compares death to changing clothes. Just as we throw away worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. The image makes death feel less like an ending and more like a transition.
en.2.43: Krishna describes people who treat scripture only as a way to gain pleasure, power and heaven. Their words are attractive but their aim is reward. A mind fixed on rewards stays restless and cannot settle into deep, steady focus.
en.4.16: Krishna says that even wise people are confused about what action is and what inaction is. He promises to explain it so that Arjuna can be free from harm. The question matters because it decides whether our work binds us or frees us.
en.4.17: Krishna explains that one must understand right action, wrong action and inaction, because the nature of action is subtle. What looks like action may not be, and what looks like rest may be deeply active. The next verses unpack this idea.
en.5.8: A person who knows the truth feels, "I am not really the doer," even while seeing, hearing, touching, eating, walking, sleeping and breathing. The senses carry on their work, while the inner self remains a witness. This removes ego from action without stopping action.
en.8.5: Krishna says that whoever leaves the body remembering him at the time of death attains his state, without doubt. The last thought reflects a lifetime of thinking. That is why the Gita stresses remembering the divine in everyday life, not only at the end.
en.10.16: Arjuna asks Krishna to describe fully the divine glories through which he pervades all the worlds. He wants concrete ways to recognise the divine in the world around him. Krishna's answer fills the rest of the chapter.
en.10.41: Krishna says that whatever is powerful, beautiful or glorious anywhere comes from a spark of his splendour. Excellence anywhere is a window to the divine. This gives us a simple practice: wherever you see greatness, remember its source.
en.11.27: Arjuna sees the warriors of both armies rushing into the cosmic form's terrible mouths, some crushed between its teeth. He is being shown the outcome of the war before it happens. The vision reveals that time is already carrying everyone towards their end.
en.11.29: Arjuna compares the warriors to moths flying fast into a blazing fire to their destruction. They rush towards their fate driven by their own choices. The image warns how blindly beings can move towards ruin.
en.11.31: Shaken, Arjuna asks the fearsome form who it really is, bows to it and begs for grace. He wants to understand its purpose. Even in terror, his first response is reverence and a sincere wish to know.
en.11.41: Arjuna remembers how casually he spoke to Krishna as a friend, calling him "Krishna", "Yadava" and "my friend" without knowing his greatness. He realises how close he has been to the divine without seeing it. The verse is full of love, humility and regret.
en.11.50: Sanjaya describes how Krishna, after speaking, returns to his familiar gentle form and comforts the frightened Arjuna. The Lord who showed the terrifying cosmic form is also the loving friend. Both are true, and he meets Arjuna in the form he can bear.
en.12.16: Krishna describes a devotee who wants nothing, is pure, skilful, unconcerned and free from anxiety, and has given up self-centred projects. Such a person works well without being driven by personal ambition. Krishna says this devotee is dear to him.
en.18.2: Krishna defines two terms. Sannyasa means giving up actions done out of desire. Tyaga means giving up attachment to the results of all actions. The final chapter builds on this distinction to explain true renunciation.
en.18.77: Sanjaya says that each time he remembers Krishna's astonishing cosmic form, he is filled with wonder and joy again and again. The Gita closes with a witness still moved by what he saw. True wisdom stays fresh each time it is remembered.

hi.6.21: इस श्लोक में उस परम सुख का वर्णन है जो इन्द्रियों से नहीं, केवल शुद्ध बुद्धि से अनुभव होता है। ध्यान में स्थित योगी जब इस आनन्द को पा लेता है, तो वह उससे कभी विचलित नहीं होता। यह सुख बाहरी वस्तुओं पर निर्भर नहीं, इसलिए स्थायी है।
